title: These Russian Mathematicians Taught AI Models How to Talk to Each Other Without Using Words
gist: Startup Mostik has built a method for AI models to exchange information directly via their internal weight representations rather than text output, letting a small open-weight model (Qwen-3.5, 4B params) approximate a much larger one (GLM-5.2, 753B params) at one-twentieth the cost with performance roughly halfway between them -- a technique that could boost the competitiveness of open-weight models against closed frontier labs and challenges the assumption that AI progress requires ever-larger monolithic models. Note: Mostik's cost/performance and ARC-AGI 3 claims are company-reported and not independently verified in the article.

insights.claim: Mostik developed a method allowing different AI models to communicate directly via the mathematical values in their weights -- rather than by generating and feeding text output between models -- letting a larger model's capabilities be transferred to a smaller model far more efficiently than traditional model-chaining.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: If validated and generalizable, weight-space model communication could reduce the compute cost of achieving frontier-level performance, undercutting the pure scaling-compute thesis that has driven massive capex at frontier labs.

insights.claim: In a demonstration, Mostik bridged the largest version of GLM-5.2 (753 billion parameters, open-weight) with a 4-billion-parameter version of Qwen-3.5 that can run on a mobile device; the resulting hybrid system cost one-twentieth of the full GLM model while delivering performance exactly halfway between the two models.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: A 20x cost reduction for roughly half the performance gap closed is a concrete, quantified efficiency data point; if it holds up under independent testing, it materially changes the cost-performance frontier calculus for deploying large open-weight models versus smaller ones.

insights.claim: A model built using Mostik's approach has risen to the top of ARC-AGI 3, a notoriously difficult AI benchmark competition -- though the company declined to disclose further details, citing an active desire to win the contest.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: A leaderboard-topping result on a hard benchmark is a strong (if unverified/self-reported and details-withheld) signal of the technique's real-world competitiveness, worth tracking as Mostik's public disclosures increase.

themes.theme: Implications for open-weight models and AI scaling strategy

insights.claim: Mostik CEO Sasha Malysheva argues the technique, if it takes off, could increase the value of open-weight models by allowing them to better compete with closed, proprietary models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: A viable technique for cheaply combining open-weight models to match closed-model performance would erode the competitive moat of closed frontier labs, a structural threat to the pricing power of OpenAI/Anthropic-style proprietary model businesses.

insights.claim: Malysheva states she does not believe the future of AI will be a single monolithic model or that capabilities will keep coming from scaling (larger models, more data), instead betting on ensembles/combinations of many models as the better path forward.
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: This is an explicit contrarian bet against the dominant industry scaling-law thesis that has justified hundreds of billions in frontier-model compute investment; if ensemble/bridging approaches prove competitive, it undercuts the return-on-capex logic behind ever-larger single-model training runs.
insights.quote: I personally do not think we will have a monolithic model [in the future] or that the capabilities of models will come from scaling.

insights.claim: Vladimir Arustamian, tech lead at AI software company Lovable, says that if Mostik enables pairing frontier models with domain-specific models (biology, physics, etc.), many more specialized models would likely be trained -- and notes Mostik achieved a working system in 'a matter of months' that he 'would have guessed was years out.'
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: An independent industry technical lead corroborating both the speed of Mostik's breakthrough and its potential to spur a wave of specialized-model development is a bullish signal for a shift toward heterogeneous, composable AI architectures over monolithic frontier models.
insights.quote: This team has been at it for a matter of months and already has something running that I would have guessed was years out.

insights.claim: Former Google DeepMind computer scientist Karl Tuyls says the Mostik technique lets users 'approach large-model quality without the large model handling the entire loop,' calling it 'a no-brainer for anyone tasked with running models as efficiently as possible.'
insights.speaker: Will Knight
insights.so_what: Independent corroboration from a former DeepMind researcher adds credibility to the efficiency claims beyond Mostik's own marketing, relevant for assessing whether this technique could see broader industry adoption for inference-cost reduction.
insights.quote: you can approach large-model quality without the large model handling the entire loop, giving you substantial improvements with just a smaller model running alongside
